consensus_summary: Multivalent biblical image whose recognized core cluster is divine judgment/wrath (especially prophetic), theophany/God’s presence and voice, life’s trials and adversities stilled by Christ, and chaotic or hostile powers subdued by divine sovereignty.
book_summary: Nations in turmoil, pictured as the raging sea that is stilled by Christ’s word “Peace, be still.”
consensus_core_identification: divine judgment/wrath, theophany, trials of life, or chaotic/hostile powers
book_core_identification: nations in turmoil (raging sea of the peoples)
boundary_disagreement: Book restricts the primary referent to geopolitical/national turmoil and de-emphasizes personal trials, the storm as instrument of judgment itself, and pure theophanic manifestation that the consensus admits as standard applications.
rationale: Consensus treats storm/tempest as a recognized multivalent cluster centered on divine power expressed as judgment, presence, testing, or chaos mastery. The book preserves the chaos/stilling motif (already present via Ps 65:7’s explicit link of seas to tumult of peoples and the Gospel sea-calming) but narrows its extension to the specific case of nations in turmoil. This is a real boundary change (excluding or sidelining the more frequent personal-trial and pure-judgment uses) without replacing the central category of restless powers under divine control. The book’s own common-view note confirms awareness of the broader consensus cluster while offering the narrower national reading.
strongest_objection: Prophetic usage most often makes the storm the vehicle of judgment rather than the nations themselves, and popular Christian application of the Gospel pericopes most often treats personal “storms of life”; the book’s national focus, though textually grounded, may over-specify one strand.
